demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I remind myself it could have been worse
I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel isolated and set apart from others
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only markedly high-risk/impulsive strategy and is poorly supported by the rest of the selected nodes. The other strategies are comparatively cognitive/obsessional (mental rituals, downward comparison), and the threat/memory/appraisal items do not show the broader dysregulation, dissociation, or severe affective overload that would make this combination clinically cohesive.

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall implies the patient was physically injured in the traumatic event. That is hard to reconcile with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another' unless she was also injured, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. The rest of the memory items emphasize fragmented retrieval and sensory reliving, but not a personally injured trauma narrative.

vignette:
Aisha, a 47-year-old architect, still found it difficult to deliberately piece together the details of the accident that had occurred almost a year ago. When she tried to access the memory, it felt like trying to grasp smoke – fragmented and elusive. Yet, in moments she least expected, vivid sensations would pierce through. She could still taste the metallic tang of fear and dust in her mouth, just as she had the moment the steel beam, dislodged by a last-minute structural change she had approved, swung wildly and struck a worker on the site. The sickening thud and the worker's scream, followed by the blare of sirens, often replayed in her mind, an auditory recall that felt as real as if they were happening again.

In the weeks and months that followed, Aisha found herself dwelling incessantly on what she had done wrong. She would replay every decision, every conversation leading up to that moment, certain that if she had just checked one more detail, or pushed back harder on the accelerated timeline, the accident would have been averted. It was a relentless self-blame rumination that consumed her thoughts. To cope, she would sometimes remind herself that it could have been worse, that the worker had survived, a downward comparison she hoped would bring some relief, but the weight of her perceived culpability remained.

Her daily life, once ordered and purposeful, had become a minefield of potential threats. Working in her downtown office, surrounded by the constant hum of city life and the occasional clang of nearby construction, had become a source of constant distress. Ordinary sounds, like a sudden car horn or the distant rumble of machinery, would make her jump or startle, reacting as if she were in immediate danger even when nothing was actually wrong. These false alarms left her perpetually on edge, making it incredibly difficult to concentrate on the intricate designs and blueprints that were once her passion. She found herself staring blankly at her computer screen, unable to focus, her mind racing with a vague sense of dread.

Aisha had developed a series of mental rituals, a form of magical prevention. Before every client meeting, before signing off on any drawing, she would silently repeat a specific sequence of numbers in her head, convinced that this internal incantation would prevent another catastrophe. This constant vigilance, coupled with her struggle to concentrate, began to affect her work. Deadlines were missed, and her once impeccable attention to detail wavered, leading to minor errors that she would then obsess over, convinced they were precursors to another disaster. She started to delegate site visits, finding increasingly elaborate excuses to avoid the very places she needed to be to oversee her projects, fearing that her presence might somehow invite misfortune.

The person Aisha had become felt utterly unrecognisable to her. The confident, decisive architect who had once thrived on complex challenges had been replaced by someone anxious and withdrawn. She often thought, "Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation," comparing herself unfavourably to an imagined, perfect version of herself who would have prevented the tragedy. This deep sense of shame and inadequacy led her to feel increasingly isolated and set apart from others. She pulled away from her colleagues, no longer engaging in the easy banter that once characterised her workplace, and even her relationship with her husband felt strained by the unspoken burden she carried.

The toll on her career and her marriage was becoming undeniable. Her husband had gently, but firmly, suggested she seek help, expressing concern for her profound change in demeanour. Aisha finally made the call, exhausted by the relentless internal battle and the constant fear of making another mistake. She came to therapy hoping to find a way back to the person she once was, or at least to a place where she could trust herself again, where the world didn't feel like a constant threat, and where she could concentrate on her work without the shadow of that terrible day looming over every decision. Most of all, she longed for a quiet mind, free from the echoes of the past and the fear of a future she felt powerless to control.
